impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating the jury's finding that Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents. The court held that the patents, which disclosed one humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibody and referenced known methods for making others, satisfied written description and enablement for claims covering the genus of humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. This decision protects Teva's patents covering the active ingredient in its Ajovy migraine drug.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biologic drug patents that claim a genus of antibodies while disclosing a representative species and known methods of production, benefiting pharmaceutical innovators seeking broad patent coverage.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates barriers for generic and biosimilar competitors seeking to invalidate genus claims in antibody patents, potentially delaying market entry of competing biologic products.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought its trade secret misappropriation claim against EOFlow, which hired former Insulet employees who shared proprietary information about Insulet's insulin patch pump.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred because the statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing. This ruling vacated a jury damages award for trade secret misappropriation related to EOFlow's development of a competing insulin patch pump using information from former Insulet employees.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces strict application of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, protecting companies from stale trade secret claims and providing certainty for businesses that hire employees from competitors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation; delay in filing suit risks losing the ability to enforce trade secret rights entirely.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's damages expert testimony and in its assessment of trade secret damages and breach of contract damages arising from Ford's development of competing software after licensing Versata's automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury award. The court affirmed the denial of Ford's JMOL on trade secret misappropriation liability. This case involves Ford's development of its own manufacturing configuration software (PDO) after licensing Versata's ACM and MCA software products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides trade secret plaintiffs with greater flexibility in presenting damages models, potentially expanding the range of recoverable damages for software trade secret misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that license third-party software and later develop competing in-house solutions face significant litigation risk, including potential trade secret misappropriation liability and substantial damages exposure.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether plaintiffs presented legally sufficient evidence to establish that each of the four asserted trade secrets was protectable under California law, and whether the jury's finding on patent inventorship was supported by sufficient evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to present sufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known in the field. The court also reversed the denial of JMOL on patent invalidity, finding that the same generally known ideas could not constitute an inventive contribution for inventorship purposes. The court affirmed the counterfeiting claim related to unauthorized use of the Penuma® trademark.
impacts.positiveImplications: Clarifies that trade secret plaintiffs must present evidence sufficient to distinguish their alleged secrets from generally known information in the relevant field, providing defendants with a meaningful basis to challenge trade secret protectability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face a higher evidentiary bar to demonstrate protectability; information that is generally known in a field cannot be shielded as a trade secret, even if the specific compilation or application was developed internally.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality principles and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory for a multicore processor patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit addressed Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's '836 patent relating to selecting processor cores for task execution in multicore chips. The court considered whether extraterritoriality bars infringement claims where key steps may occur outside the United States and whether VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory was properly rejected. The ruling partially reversed and remanded, clarifying the application of extraterritoriality principles and damages discovery obligations in patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides guidance on the territorial scope of U.S. patent infringement claims for semiconductor and technology companies with global design and manufacturing operations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies must carefully analyze the geographic location of each claimed method step, as extraterritoriality may bar infringement claims where significant activities occur outside the U.S.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility under § 101 for certain asserted patents relating to non-uniform constellation designs used in television broadcasting, while affirming eligibility for other patents. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. This case has significant implications for the consumer electronics industry, as the patents relate to the ATSC 3.0 digital broadcasting standard used in televisions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Affirms that some communications technology patents involving non-uniform constellations survive § 101 challenges, supporting patent holders asserting standard-essential or standard-related patents against major electronics manufacturers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing industry standards face continued exposure to patent infringement claims, with this decision confirming that certain standard-related patent claims survive eligibility challenges.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' between a provisional patent application and a non-provisional application constituted correction of an obvious typographical error that preserved the priority date, or introduced new matter that broke the priority chain and rendered the patent anticipated by Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's '953 patent directed to coronavirus protease inhibitors, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in the alkyl group definition was not an obvious typographical error and therefore the patent could not claim priority from the earlier provisional application. Because the priority chain was broken, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the claims. This decision effectively removes Enanta's patent challenge to Pfizer's blockbuster Paxlovid COVID-19 treatment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects Pfizer's ability to market Paxlovid without paying royalties to Enanta, and reinforces the importance of precision in provisional patent applications for all pharmaceutical companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies face severe consequences from even minor errors in provisional applications; a single character difference in a chemical formula definition can destroy priority and invalidate an entire patent family.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in its jury instructions and verdict form by using a single infringement question covering all four asserted patents and in its § 101 analysis of wireless building automation system patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, holding that the verdict form's use of a single question on infringement covering all four asserted patents was prejudicial error. The court also vacated and remanded for further § 101 proceedings under Alice step two for the '495 patent while affirming eligibility for the '887 and '371 patents. This case involves patents on wireless communications in building automation systems used by ecobee's smart thermostat products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides important procedural protection requiring patent-specific verdict forms in multi-patent infringement cases, ensuring accused infringers receive individualized consideration of each asserted patent.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents face stricter requirements for jury verdict forms, increasing procedural complexity and the risk of retrials in multi-patent cases.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds that were not included in its 2016 IPR petition but could have been discovered through a reasonably diligent search.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to support estoppel on one ground and that the district court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other ground. The court emphasized that the 'reasonably could have raised' standard under § 315(e)(2) must be applied carefully to avoid penalizing petitioners based on post-hoc knowledge of potentially invalidating prior art.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides meaningful protection for IPR petitioners against overly broad estoppel, ensuring that companies are not unfairly barred from asserting invalidity defenses based on prior art that was not reasonably discoverable at the time of the petition.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent owners face a higher burden to invoke IPR estoppel, as courts must carefully evaluate the reasonableness of prior art searches without the benefit of hindsight.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly held that testimony of a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative is admissible at summary judgment even when the representative lacks personal knowledge, and whether the pre-AIA on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that prior art sales expressly disclose the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible regardless of personal knowledge and that source code constitutes non-hearsay computer commands. The court rejected the argument that the on-sale bar requires express disclosure of functionality in commercial sales, confirming that commercial sale of a device embodying the claimed invention is sufficient to trigger the bar even without public disclosure of internal functionality.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens the evidentiary tools available to patent challengers by confirming the broad admissibility of 30(b)(6) testimony and source code evidence, and clarifies that commercial sales of prior art devices trigger the on-sale bar without requiring disclosure of internal functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face broader invalidity exposure, as competitors can rely on 30(b)(6) testimony from representatives without personal knowledge and need not show that prior art sales disclosed the specific claimed functionality.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case was exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's asserted claims relating to automated farming data collection systems were patent-ineligible under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional under § 285. The court found that claims directed to capturing and processing farming operation data using relay devices on equipment were abstract ideas without an inventive concept sufficient to survive the Alice framework.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides a potential basis for exceptional-case attorney fee awards in agricultural technology patent cases where § 101 issues are clear, discouraging assertion of likely ineligible patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Agricultural technology companies seeking to patent data collection and processing methods on farming equipment face significant § 101 hurdles, limiting patent protection for precision agriculture innovations.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights to a licensee but retains the right to independently sue for infringement retains sufficient constitutional standing to bring patent infringement claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner retains constitutional standing to sue for infringement when it retains the right to independently bring suit against third-party infringers, even after granting an exclusive license for commercialization. The court found that this retained exclusionary right satisfies the irreducible constitutional minimum of standing regardless of the breadth of the license granted.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring exclusive licenses can retain standing to enforce patents by preserving independent enforcement rights, providing flexibility in licensing arrangements while maintaining the ability to sue infringers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers cannot as easily defeat patent suits by arguing the patent owner lacks standing due to an exclusive license, as retained enforcement rights will suffice for constitutional standing.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents are invalid for omission of a coinventor under 35 U.S.C. § 256 when the patent owner acknowledges the coinventor's contributions but is unable to locate the omitted coinventor to correct inventorship.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the patents were invalid for failure to name a coinventor, where the patent owner acknowledged the coinventor's contributions but could not locate him to add him via § 256(a). The court also affirmed the denial of judicial correction under § 256(b), finding the patent owner had not met its burden. This case highlights the critical importance of proper inventorship identification, particularly when working with foreign manufacturing partners who contribute to the inventive process.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign manufacturers on product development face invalidation risk if manufacturing partners contribute to the invention but cannot later be located for inventorship correction; businesses must document and preserve contact information for all potential coinventors.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported when the IPR petition was filed by a non-party to underlying litigation on the petitioned patent owner's filing deadline, and whether the Board erred in its obviousness analysis of sensor-based logistics system patent claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The court addressed the concerning practice of third parties filing IPR petitions on behalf of or in coordination with parties in underlying litigation to circumvent the one-year time bar under § 315(b). The court also found errors in the Board's obviousness analysis regarding claims directed to restricting access to sensor information after a predetermined time delay.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners gain additional protection against potentially coordinated IPR filings by third parties acting as proxies for time-barred litigants, and benefit from closer scrutiny of Board obviousness findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR as a defense strategy must ensure compliance with the time bar and avoid coordination with third-party petitioners, or risk having invalidity determinations vacated.

impacts.caseName: Fuente Marketing Ltd. v. Vaporous Technologies, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the TTAB correctly found no likelihood of confusion between Fuente's registered standard character 'X' trademarks for cigars and Vaporous's stylized X-and-dot mark for oral vaporizers, despite overlapping channels of trade in smoking-related products.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the TTAB's dismissal of Fuente's trademark opposition, finding no likelihood of confusion despite some overlap in goods and trade channels. The Board found that the dissimilarity of the marks outweighed the relatedness of the goods. This decision provides guidance on likelihood of confusion analysis for single-letter marks in adjacent product categories within the smoking/vaping industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies in adjacent product categories can more confidently adopt marks with common elements (such as single letters) when the overall commercial impression of the marks differs substantially.
impacts.negativeImplications: Owners of simple single-letter trademarks may find it difficult to prevent registration of stylized marks incorporating the same letter in related product categories, even where channels of trade overlap.
